claims.text: Applying a controlled, uniform copper nanolayer to tungsten particle surfaces before consolidation will reduce interfacial electron scattering.
Reduced interfacial electron scattering will enhance the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The copper nanolayer intervention will retain the mechanical durability and irradiation resistance associated with the tungsten framework.
The proposed copper coating thickness is 5–20 nm.
The copper nanolayer can be applied by electroless plating before consolidation.
Rapid spark plasma sintering at 1200–1300 °C in an inert atmosphere will minimize oxidation and defect generation.
A thin copper interlayer at W–Cu interfaces promotes direct metallic bonding.
A thin copper interlayer at W–Cu interfaces reduces thermal boundary resistance.
The copper nanolayer bridges the tungsten particles and the bulk copper phase.
Bridging the tungsten and bulk copper phases enhances electron coupling across the interface.
Enhanced interfacial electron coupling reduces thermal boundary resistance and interfacial scattering.
The copper nanolayer does not alter the bulk mechanical properties of tungsten.
Avoiding alteration of tungsten's bulk mechanical properties preserves irradiation resistance and structural integrity.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher directional thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The coated composite will maintain mechanical durability comparable to that of an unmodified W–Cu composite.
The coated composite will maintain irradiation stability comparable to that of an unmodified W–Cu composite.
The intervention's efficacy depends on achieving an optimal and uniform copper coating thickness.
Non-uniform coatings may produce inconsistent property improvements.
Scale-up challenges may limit the thermal-conductivity improvement.
